title: The Case of the Missing Lantern Ribbons
markdown:
In the deep valleys of Hazelhowe, wind whispered through tall pines and sunlight danced on old stones. Aeron was a young elf with bright watchful eyes, like forest pools after rain, a heart brave and steady as a badger’s, fast on his feet and faster with a curious question.

His very best friend was Ember, a baby dragon, fluffy, about the size of a large cuddly dog, scales shimmering with all the colours of a sunset. Ember let out little puffs of smoke when excited, or worried, or sometimes just because. Ember was often excited.

One evening the sun painted the mountains pink and gold. Whisperwind was getting ready for its favourite yearly event: the Lantern Festival. Usually the village sparkled, each lantern with long flowing ribbons that danced like happy fireflies.

On the village green the lanterns were hung, but bare. All the beautiful colourful ribbons gone. Vanished. Poof. Not a fun trick.

“Where could they be?” Sad plain lanterns, naked without their decorations.

Ember puffed a small worried cloud around his snout.

“Don’t worry. We’ll find them. Best clue-finders in Hazelhowe. Let’s look.”

Past the babbling stream, cool and clear. Near the old Whispering Willow, branches like hushed secrets. Clues can be tiny, like a dropped berry, or odd, like a stack of mushrooms. Near mossy rocks where shadows played hide-and-seek: a tall wobbly tower of plump purple toadstools, stacked perfectly. You didn’t see that every day.

“Who would do that?”

Ember sniffed, nudged Aeron’s hand, pointed a tiny sharp claw toward a narrow path up the steep valley side.

“That way? Good thinking, my little smoke-puff.”

The path wound like a sleepy snake. Air wonderfully sweet and buzzy, a thousand tiny flowers. Then a low rumbling growl that seemed to shake the ground.

“Oh, that sounds big.” Ember held closer. A nervous wispy cloud.

They peeked around a grey boulder like a sleeping giant. Happily munching a juicy apple: a truly enormous ogre, wide as a small cottage, colourful stained apron, no grumpy look. An ogre beekeeper. Dozens of humming hives clung to rocky walls. Kind though gruff, brow deep in thought, carefully moving a hive, humming a low rumbling tune.

“Excuse me, sir!” A little shaky, clear.

The ogre jumped, surprising for someone so big, then looked down with wide friendly eyes. “Bless my bristly beard! Tiny little things, like crumbs fallen off a biscuit!” A laugh like a small avalanche.

“Aeron and Ember. We’re looking for missing lantern ribbons. Bright and colourful. And we saw strangely stacked mushrooms near the path.”

He scratched a stubbly head with a finger thick as a tree branch. “Mushrooms? Aye. Needed something sturdy to hold my spare honey jars. Can’t have those tumbling down the ravine.” Chuckle. “Ribbons? Bright fluttery things? My littlest bees, the especially mischievous ones, they’ve been taking bits and bobs. Excited about shiny things. Collecting nectar from special moon-blossoms up high. They must have taken your ribbons for their nests. They do love a bit of decoration.”

A big clumsy finger, surprisingly steady, toward a hidden cave behind a shimmering waterfall, a silver curtain. “Buzzing in and out all afternoon. Be careful. They get a bit buzzy if you startle them.”

“Thank you so much, Mr. Ogre Beekeeper!”

“Just call me Bartholomew.” A wink that crinkled his whole face. “Good luck with those little busybodies.”

Bounce in their steps toward the waterfall. Soft constant hum of tiny wings. Behind the cool misty curtain: dim, and Ember squeaked with delight.

Gently hanging from rough cave walls, woven into golden honeycomb homes: all the missing lantern ribbons. Pretty bows, lining little bee-houses, draped like tiny colourful flags. Cozy. Festive.

“They’re so pretty. But the villagers need them for the festival.”

He could not just take them. These were homes. He remembered sweet juicy berries near the cave entrance, the ones the bees loved. A large pile of the plumpest, placed near the honeycomb.

“Here, little bees. Have these instead. Much tastier than ribbons. A special treat for all your hard work.”

Antennae twitching. Friendly louder buzzing. They left the ribbons almost free for the unexpected feast. Aeron and Ember, gentle hands and tiny claws, untangled each ribbon, quiet as falling leaves. Ember puffed happy contented smoke that sparkled in the dim.

All the ribbons in Aeron’s arms. A grateful nod. Down the valley. The villagers of Whisperwind, who had looked quite glum, cheered and clapped.

That night the Lantern Festival was the most beautiful anyone in Hazelhowe had ever seen. Warm inviting light. Ribbons dancing in the mountain breeze. A shower of captured stars. Aeron and Ember sat on the village green.

“We did it, Ember.”

A nudge to the cheek. A contented puff rose into the night, mixing with the starlight, and Bartholomew’s hives, far up the valley, hummed along, which was a kind of applause.
